title: Tasks, Launch Modes & Back Stack
scopeHtml: Scope: the task/back stack model, launchMode and Intent flags, taskAffinity, onNewIntent, notification back stacks, recents, back handling and predictive back, and Activity transitions (briefly). Intents/PendingIntent mechanics are in the Intents chunk; Navigation deep links are in A4.

questions.promptHtml: What is a "task" in Android, and how does it relate to the back stack and to the process? Can one app have several tasks, and can one task hold activities from several apps?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Everything about launch modes and "why did Back go there?" depends on this mental model. Candidates who equate task = process or task = app cannot reason about launch bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A task is a stack of activities the user experiences as one unit of work, and the back stack is that stack: last in, first out. A task is a UI/navigation concept owned by the system server (ATMS), not a process. One app can have several tasks, and a task can contain activities from different apps, for example my app launches the system share sheet or a camera activity into the same task, and Back returns through them in order.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• A task is a collection of activities arranged in a stack. The activity that started the task is the root; the most recently started is on top. Back pops the top one (finishes it) and resumes the one below.
  • Tasks live in the system_server (ActivityTaskManagerService). Your process only hosts activity instances. Two activities in the same task can run in different processes (android:process), and two tasks can be served by one process.
  • Each task shows as one card in Recents. Moving a task to the background keeps the whole stack intact (the stack is state in system_server, not in your process), which is why a task can survive the process being killed: the stack entries remain, and the system re-creates the process and the top activity on return (see the process death chunk).
  • Which task a new activity goes to is decided at launch from: the launchMode of the target, the Intent flags, and the target's taskAffinity. By default (standard mode, no flags) the new activity joins the caller's task.
  • Activities from other apps join your task when you start them without NEW_TASK, because the unit is the task, not the package. That is why the system "Pick a file" screen appears and Back returns to you cleanly.
Task A (my app)              Task B (another app)
+-----------------+          +-----------------+
| DetailActivity  | <- top   | ComposeActivity | <- top
| ListActivity    |          | InboxActivity   | <- root
| MainActivity    | <- root  +-----------------+
+-----------------+
Back: Detail finishes -> List resumes -> Main -> (task empty) -> previous task / launcher

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Inspect the real stack, the fastest way to debug any launch-mode problem
// adb shell dumpsys activity activities | grep -E "Task|ActivityRecord"
// adb shell am stack list   (older releases)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "one app = one task". Same app can have many tasks (NEW_TASK, different affinity, multi-window, documents).
  • Saying the back stack lives in your process. It is system_server state; the process can be dead while the stack entries remain.
  • Forgetting that Back from the root activity does not always finish the app (see the Android 12 root-activity question).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does the stack go when the process is killed? → It stays in system_server; on return the system re-creates the process and the top activity, restoring from saved state. Activities below are created lazily when Back reaches them.
  2. Does Home destroy the task? → No. The task moves to the background as a whole; activities go through onStop.
  3. Is Back stack order the same as the order of onCreate calls? → Yes for ordinary launches, but singleTask/CLEAR_TOP can pop entries off the top, so stack order is not the same as history of launches.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "stack of activities, Back pops". The senior answer says the stack is system_server state independent of the process, explains that task selection is a function of launchMode, flags and affinity, and can use dumpsys activity activities to prove what actually happened.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams debugging "Back goes to the wrong screen" without ever dumping the stack burn days guessing; the dump usually shows the answer in one screen.

questions.promptHtml: What are standard and singleTop launch modes? What happens when I start an activity that is already on top of the stack in each mode?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the entry-level check that you know launch modes affect instance counts and that onNewIntent exists.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In standard every startActivity creates a new instance on top of the caller's task, even if the same class is already on top. In singleTop, if an instance of that activity is already at the top of the task, the system does not create a new one; it delivers the new Intent to the existing instance via onNewIntent(). If the instance exists but is not on top, singleTop behaves like standard and creates a new one.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• standard (default): new instance per launch, in the task of the caller. Stack A,B + start B → A,B,B.
  • singleTop: check only the top of the target task. Top is B and B is singleTop → deliver to it. Stack A,B,C + start B → A,B,C,B (not on top, so a new instance).
  • Delivery order for a reused singleTop on top: onNewIntent() then, if it was in the background, onRestart/onStart/onResume. If it is already resumed, only onNewIntent() (and onResume does not run again).
  • The same effect can be requested per call with FLAG_ACTIVITY_SINGLE_TOP without changing the manifest.
  • Use case: search result screen, notification-driven screen, or any screen where double-tap on a button could stack two copies.
singleTop B, start B with stack [A, B]  -> [A, B]       onNewIntent(B)
singleTop B, start B with stack [A, B, C] -> [A, B, C, B]  new instance

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<activity
    android:name=".SearchActivity"
    android:launchMode="singleTop" />
override fun onNewIntent(intent: Intent) {
    super.onNewIntent(intent)
    setIntent(intent) // otherwise getIntent() returns the OLD intent
    handleQuery(intent.getStringExtra("q"))
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting setIntent(intent); later code reading getIntent() sees stale data.
  • Assuming singleTop dedupes anywhere in the stack. It only checks the top.
  • Reading data only in onCreate; with singleTop the activity may never be recreated for a new request.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a double-tap crash if two startActivity calls fire fast? → With standard you can get two instances before the first one is on top; singleTop on the target (or a debounce) prevents it.
  2. Is onNewIntent called on first launch? → No, onCreate is. onNewIntent is only for reuse.
  3. Who owns the data in a reused activity's ViewModel? → The existing ViewModel stays; you must reset or re-key it for the new request in onNewIntent.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "singleTop reuses if on top". Senior adds: top-of-task-only rule, setIntent, state reset for ViewModel, redelivery of the stale intent on rotation, and the per-call flag alternative.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Double-tap on a notification action created two identical "Order details" screens; a one-line singleTop plus handling in onNewIntent fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: How does singleTask differ from singleTop? What happens to the activities above an existing singleTask instance?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: singleTask is used for "home" activities and has destructive semantics (it pops the stack). Misuse destroys user state.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: singleTask means one instance of the activity in the system for its affinity's task. If it already exists, the system brings its task to the foreground, finishes every activity above it, and delivers the intent through onNewIntent(). If it does not exist, it creates it in the task matching its affinity, becoming the root if a new task had to be created. Unlike singleTop, it does not care whether the instance is on top, and it clears what is above.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Lookup is by task affinity (default = package name) and component, not only by the caller's task. That is how the intent can pull a different task to the front.
  • Equivalent to CLEAR_TOP + SINGLE_TOP semantics on the existing instance, plus cross-task lookup.
  • Other activities can still be pushed on top of a singleTask activity within that task (it is not exclusive; that is singleInstance).
  • Stack [Main(singleTask), List, Detail], start Main → [Main], Detail and List are finished (onDestroy), and Main gets onNewIntent.
  • Because of the cross-task and clearing behavior, FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK is not required for it to route into its own task, but it is typically combined when starting from a non-Activity context.
  • Risk: a notification that targets a singleTask Main wipes the user's current deep flow (checkout steps) with no warning.
[Main*, List, Detail] + start Main(singleTask)
 -> List, Detail finished
 -> [Main*]  onNewIntent()

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<activity
    android:name=".MainActivity"
    android:launchMode="singleTask"
    android:exported="true">
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER" />
    </intent-filter>
</activity>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using singleTask on a leaf screen (Detail) so everything above vanishes unexpectedly.
  • Forgetting that the destroyed activities lose in-memory state unless persisted.
  • Expecting startActivityForResult semantics to be unchanged across tasks; results do not behave like a same-task start (prefer in-task design or non-result communication).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. singleTask vs CLEAR_TOP|SINGLE_TOP? → Same effect on one task, but the flag is per call and works inside the caller's task; singleTask is a manifest-level contract and cross-task.
  2. Does singleTask guarantee only one instance forever? → One instance per task that matches; with multiple tasks (different affinity, API 31 singleInstancePerTask, multi-window with MULTIPLE_TASK) you can have more.
  3. Back from the root singleTask? → Falls to whatever is below the task, such as the Launcher (and Android 12 root-activity behavior applies).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "only one instance". Senior: mentions affinity-based lookup, the destructive pop of everything above, the loss of "return to caller" behaviour, and picks it only for true hub screens.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team switched Main to singleTask to fix duplicates and began receiving "I lost my cart" tickets, because notification taps cleared the checkout activities above Main.

questions.promptHtml: onBackPressed() is deprecated. What replaces it, and why was it replaced?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Back handling touched every app because of predictive back. Tests whether you know the AndroidX dispatcher and the platform change.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Activity.onBackPressed() is deprecated from API 33. The replacement is OnBackPressedDispatcher from androidx.activity (1.0+), which I use through onBackPressedDispatcher.addCallback(owner) { ... } with an OnBackPressedCallback. It was replaced because the old model is a synchronous "the user pressed back, do whatever" call that the system cannot predict, so it cannot animate or cancel the back gesture; predictive back needs a registered, enableable callback the system can query before the gesture finishes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Old model: KEYCODE_BACK key event → onBackPressed(). The system only knows the outcome after you finished the action.
  • New model: components register callbacks; each callback has an isEnabled flag. The system knows "does anyone intercept Back?" in advance. If nobody does, it can play the system animation (back to home, cross-activity). Platform side: OnBackInvokedDispatcher and OnBackInvokedCallback (API 33).
  • AndroidX ComponentActivity bridges it: on API 33+ it registers with the platform dispatcher; on older releases it falls back to the key event path.
  • Dispatch order: last-added enabled callback runs first (LIFO). If none handles, default: finish the activity (or pop the fragment back stack entry via FragmentManager's own callback).
  • Opt-in is a manifest flag, android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback="true" (see the predictive back question).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class EditorActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val confirmDiscard = object : OnBackPressedCallback(enabled = false) {
        override fun handleOnBackPressed() {
            showDiscardDialog { isEnabled = false; onBackPressedDispatcher.onBackPressed() }
        }
    }
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        onBackPressedDispatcher.addCallback(this, confirmDiscard) // lifecycle-aware
        viewModel.dirty.observe(this) { confirmDiscard.isEnabled = it }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Leaving a callback permanently enabled; it swallows Back for the whole screen.
  • Calling onBackPressedDispatcher.onBackPressed() while your own callback is still enabled; infinite loop. Disable first, then call it.
  • Overriding onKeyDown(KEYCODE_BACK); with opt-in it will not be called.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does the owner parameter matter? → Yes. The callback is only registered while the owner is at least STARTED and removed on DESTROYED.
  2. Which callback wins? → The most recently added enabled one, LIFO.
  3. How do Fragments handle it? → The FragmentManager's back stack pop is just one more callback registered by the host.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use OnBackPressedCallback". Senior: explains the model change (predictable intercept state for the system), LIFO ordering, enable-state-driven design, and the manifest opt-in.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A screen with "unsaved changes?" logic written in onBackPressed stopped working after the app opted in to predictive back, because the override was never called.

questions.promptHtml: What are singleInstance and singleInstancePerTask? When would you ever use them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who memorised four names from those who know the exclusivity differences and the API 31 addition.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: singleInstance makes the activity the only member of its own task: it is always the root and nothing else ever joins that task; anything it starts goes to another task. singleInstancePerTask (API 31) is like singleTask, but allows multiple instances if they live in different tasks (for example with FLAG_ACTIVITY_MULTIPLE_TASK or NEW_DOCUMENT); within one task there is only one. I use them rarely: launcher-like or overlay-like hosts, picture-in-picture host, or per-document tasks on large screens.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• singleInstance: exclusive task. Starting any other activity from it uses NEW_TASK implicitly, so other activities appear in a different task and Back visits the singleInstance task as a separate card in Recents.
  • singleInstancePerTask (Android 12, API 31): the "one per task" refinement. It is the right tool for the multi-window/multi-document case (one editor window per document) where singleTask would force a single global instance.
  • Compare:
Mode Instances Task sharing Clears above onNewIntent
standard many joins caller task no no
singleTop many; reuse if on top caller task no if on top
singleTask one per matching task others may join yes yes
singleInstance one in system none; exclusive n/a yes
singleInstancePerTask one per task others may join yes yes
  • Exclusive tasks make Back confusing: finishing the activity may return the user to some unrelated task. Test on multi-window/foldables where tasks are visible side by side.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<activity
    android:name=".DocumentEditorActivity"
    android:launchMode="singleInstancePerTask"
    android:documentLaunchMode="intoExisting" />
// Open a second editor window for another document
startActivity(Intent(this, DocumentEditorActivity::class.java).apply {
    addFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_DOCUMENT or Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_MULTIPLE_TASK)
    putExtra("docId", id)
})

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using singleInstance as a "safe singleton" for a normal screen; the user ends up with an extra card in Recents and odd Back.
  • Assuming singleInstancePerTask exists below API 31; it needs a minSdk check or a fallback.
  • Expecting startActivityForResult to be smooth across the task boundary.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not singleTask for editor windows? → It would force one editor instance globally, so a second document would clear the first.
  2. How does Back behave in a singleInstance task? → It pops that single activity and then goes to the task below in the system's order, which can surprise users.
  3. Is singleInstancePerTask safe on API 30 devices? → The attribute is unknown there and the activity behaves as standard; guard design accordingly. Verify against current docs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: recites names. Senior: ties modes to a real use (multi-window documents), knows API 31, and weighs UX cost of extra Recents cards.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An "overlay" activity set to singleInstance created a phantom task in Recents on every launch; moving it to a Service-hosted window removed the complaints.

questions.promptHtml: Explain FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK, FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TOP, FLAG_ACTIVITY_SINGLE_TOP and FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK. How do they combine, and which combinations are valid?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Logout, notification and deep-link code all hinge on these flags. Wrong combos cause either duplicates or destroyed state.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: NEW_TASK starts the activity in a task matching its affinity (it does not always make a brand-new task; it reuses a matching one). CLEAR_TOP brings an existing instance to the top and finishes everything above it. SINGLE_TOP is the per-call version of singleTop. CLEAR_TASK empties the whole task before the activity starts, and is only valid together with NEW_TASK. A typical logout is NEW_TASK | CLEAR_TASK; "go back to Home screen" is CLEAR_TOP | SINGLE_TOP.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• NEW_TASK: required when starting an activity from a non-Activity Context (Application, Service). If a task with the matching affinity exists, it is brought forward and the activity is added on top (or reused if the instance exists and the mode says so). Many people expect a new empty task; usually they get the old one.
  • CLEAR_TOP: for a standard-mode target, the existing instance is destroyed and recreated (the new Intent goes to a new instance) unless combined with SINGLE_TOP, in which case it gets onNewIntent. For singleTop/singleTask targets the existing instance receives onNewIntent.
  • CLEAR_TASK + NEW_TASK: finishes every activity in the matched task, then launches the target as the new root. Without NEW_TASK the documentation says it is not valid; do not rely on it.
  • FLAG_ACTIVITY_REORDER_TO_FRONT: moves an existing instance to the top without clearing.
  • FLAG_ACTIVITY_NO_HISTORY, FLAG_ACTIVITY_EXCLUDE_FROM_RECENTS: lifetime/Recents tweaks.
Goal Flags
Logout to Login NEW_TASK + CLEAR_TASK
Pop back to existing Home, reuse it CLEAR_TOP + SINGLE_TOP
Start from Service/Application NEW_TASK
Bring existing to front, keep stack REORDER_TO_FRONT

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun Context.goHomeKeepingInstance() = startActivity(
    Intent(this, HomeActivity::class.java)
        .addFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TOP or Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_SINGLE_TOP)
)

fun Context.restartAtLogin() = startActivity(
    Intent(this, LoginActivity::class.java)
        .addFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK or Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK)
)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• CLEAR_TOP alone with a standard activity: the old instance is destroyed and a fresh one created, losing its in-memory state and ViewModel.
  • Using only CLEAR_TASK.
  • Assuming NEW_TASK always creates a second task; with the same affinity it re-enters the existing one.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Flags vs manifest launchMode: which wins? → Flags set by the caller generally override the target's manifest launchMode for that launch (except for singleInstance/singleTask requirements, which the manifest dictates).
  2. Why is NEW_TASK needed from Application context? → There is no task to join, so the system throws AndroidRuntimeException: Calling startActivity() from outside of an Activity context requires FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK.
  3. How would you reproduce a duplicate-instance bug? → Launch via adb shell am start -n pkg/.Activity with -f flag values and dump the stack.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: lists flag names. Senior: knows NEW_TASK is affinity lookup, the CLEAR_TOP recreate behaviour, the CLEAR_TASK dependency, and who wins (caller flags vs manifest).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "Home" button helper using only CLEAR_TOP recreated the Home screen on every tap and re-fired its network calls; adding SINGLE_TOP removed the reload.

questions.promptHtml: When is onNewIntent() called, where does it sit in the lifecycle, and how do you handle it correctly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Almost every deep-link, notification and search bug on reused activities lives here.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: onNewIntent() is called on an existing instance when it is re-targeted instead of re-created: singleTop on top, singleTask/singleInstance, or CLEAR_TOP/SINGLE_TOP flags. If the activity was in the background, the order is onNewIntent → onRestart → onStart → onResume; if resumed, only onNewIntent. I always call setIntent(intent), reset any per-request state, and route through one shared handler used by onCreate as well.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• getIntent() returns the intent that created the activity (or the last one set with setIntent). onNewIntent does not update it. Anything that later reads getIntent() (including libraries such as Navigation handleDeepLink, analytics, or code in onResume) sees the old one unless you call setIntent.
  • Because the activity is being reused, its ViewModel, fragments and scroll positions are still the old ones. The new request must be applied on top, which is easy to get wrong if onCreate assumed a fresh screen.
  • Redelivery: after rotation or process death the system recreates the activity with its original launch intent (or the last setIntented one). An action that is not idempotent (open dialog, navigate, charge) will replay unless you mark it consumed (saved state flag, or clear the extra).
  • Lifecycle position: delivery can happen while the activity is paused/stopped; do not assume views are visible. Defer UI work until STARTED if needed.
  • Compose or Navigation host: pass the new intent into navController.handleDeepLink(intent).
Background, singleTop:  onNewIntent -> onRestart -> onStart -> onResume
Resumed, singleTop:     onNewIntent
New instance:           onCreate(intent) -> onStart -> onResume

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        if (savedInstanceState == null) route(intent) // not on rotation: avoid replay
    }
    override fun onNewIntent(intent: Intent) {
        super.onNewIntent(intent)
        setIntent(intent)
        route(intent)
    }
    private fun route(i: Intent) { /* one handler for both paths */ }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Skipping setIntent.
  • Handling the intent in onCreate only.
  • Replaying the same deep link after rotation because savedInstanceState was ignored.
  • Doing fragment transactions in onNewIntent when the state is already saved (use commit variants carefully; see the fragments chunk).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is onNewIntent called after process death? → No; the new process gets onCreate with the original intent.
  2. Why is if (savedInstanceState == null) used? → To stop replays on config change; but it also skips handling if you want the intent processed after process death; decide by whether the action is idempotent.
  3. How would you test it? → adb shell am start -n pkg/.Main --es q test twice and watch logs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "called when activity is reused". Senior: lifecycle ordering, setIntent, idempotency/replay, ViewModel reuse.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A search screen showed the previous query when launched from a second voice search; getIntent() was never updated.

questions.contextHtml:
A food-delivery app (1.4M DAU) has OrderTrackingActivity with launchMode="singleTop". Push notifications deep link to it with an orderId extra. QA reports: when a user has order 1001 open and taps a notification for order 1002, the title changes to 1002 but the map and ETA still show 1001; after rotating, it jumps back to 1001. Crash rate is unchanged, so it was triaged as cosmetic. Here is the code:

class OrderTrackingActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val vm: TrackingViewModel by viewModels()

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_tracking)
        vm.load(intent.getStringExtra("orderId")!!)
    }

    override fun onNewIntent(intent: Intent) {
        super.onNewIntent(intent)
        title = "Order " + intent.getStringExtra("orderId")
    }

    override fun onResume() {
        super.onResume()
        analytics.track("order_viewed", intent.getStringExtra("orderId"))
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, how would you reproduce it, and what is the right fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Call load again in onNewIntent." That fixes the screen but misses that getIntent() is stale (analytics logs 1001 twice, rotation restores 1001), and that the ViewModel is the same instance and may still hold a loading job and old state.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the app reproducible with adb, so I can bypass FCM? Does it happen only when the activity is open (singleTop reuse), not cold? Is the order id part of a ViewModel key or only an intent extra? Are analytics numbers inflated for repeated order views?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I would patch behind a quick release: set the intent and reload.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) onNewIntent does not call setIntent, so getIntent() returns 1001; (b) the ViewModel keeps its 1001 state and its loader is not re-keyed; (c) rotation recreates the activity with the saved original intent; (d) red herring: the map fragment caching tiles.
  4. How I'd verify each: adb shell am start -n pkg/.OrderTrackingActivity --es orderId 1001, then again with 1002; log intent in onResume; rotate and watch the VM; adb shell dumpsys activity activities to confirm a single instance (singleTop reuse working).
  5. Root cause: singleTop reuses the instance, so only onNewIntent runs. getIntent() is not updated by the framework, so onResume analytics reads the old id, and recreation restores the old intent. onCreate is the only place that starts loading.
  6. Fix: short-term:
override fun onNewIntent(intent: Intent) {
    super.onNewIntent(intent)
    setIntent(intent)
    vm.load(intent.getStringExtra("orderId")!!) // idempotent: ignores same id, cancels previous job
}

Make TrackingViewModel.load(id) cancel any in-flight job and ignore repeated ids. Move the analytics call to where the id changes (inside load result) rather than onResume, which also fires on every return from background. Long-term: derive the id from state (a SavedStateHandle key) not from getIntent(). 7. Prevention: an instrumentation test that launches the activity twice with different extras; lint/review rule "every activity with non-standard launchMode implements onNewIntent via the same handler as onCreate". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not switch to standard (that creates stacked order screens); I would not recreate the activity with recreate() (loses transitions and flickers).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the same notification is tapped twice? → load ignores the same id; the intent is idempotent.
  • What if the user taps while the app is in Recents with process dead? → New process, onCreate runs with the new intent; no onNewIntent.
  • What if analytics must count each notification open once? → Count at notification-handling time, not in onResume.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A tracking screen for a logistics product showed stale driver positions for a week; the real cause was a library reading getIntent() in onResume while the app only updated the VM. A single setIntent line fixed what two sprints of map debugging could not.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only reloads data and does not mention stale getIntent() or rotation.
  • Hire: identifies setIntent, ViewModel reload, and reproduces with adb.
  • Strong hire: addresses idempotency, analytics in onResume, saved-state design, and tests for reuse.

questions.promptHtml: What is taskAffinity, what is its default, and what do allowTaskReparenting and taskAffinity="" do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Affinity is the reason activities land in surprising tasks, and a common source of "app appears twice in Recents".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: taskAffinity is a string saying which task an activity prefers to live in. The default is the application's package name (or the taskAffinity set on <application>), so by default all activities share one affinity and one task. It only matters in two cases: when the activity is launched with NEW_TASK (the system finds a task with a matching affinity or creates one) and when allowTaskReparenting is true (the activity can move to its affinity's task later). Setting taskAffinity="" gives the activity no affinity.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Affinity does nothing for ordinary startActivity without NEW_TASK; the activity just joins the caller's task.
  • A task's own affinity comes from its root activity.
  • NEW_TASK + same affinity as an existing task → reuse that task. NEW_TASK + different affinity → new task. This is how an "overlay/share-receiver" activity becomes its own card: give it a distinct affinity.
  • allowTaskReparenting="true": if activity X (affinity "a.b") was started inside another app's task, when a task with affinity "a.b" comes to the foreground, X moves there. Classic example: a weather activity started from an email app moves to the weather app's task when the user opens the weather app. Rarely used today and can be surprising.
  • Gotcha: copy-pasted affinity on a library or debug activity can leave a stray task.
<application android:taskAffinity="com.example.app">
    <activity android:name=".ShareReceiverActivity"
        android:taskAffinity=""
        android:excludeFromRecents="true"
        android:launchMode="singleInstancePerTask" />
</application>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing affinity separates tasks for normal navigation.
  • Setting a different affinity on a deep-link target, causing launch from browsers to create a separate task with its own Back history.
  • Using taskAffinity without NEW_TASK or a mode (singleTask) that triggers lookup, and wondering why nothing changes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is the default when the manifest is silent? → Package name from <application>.
  2. How can two of my activities end up in different tasks? → Different affinity plus NEW_TASK/singleTask, or singleInstance.
  3. Does applicationId change the affinity? → The default uses the manifest package/namespace as seen by the system for that app (the applicationId at runtime); keep it consistent across flavors.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "task grouping preference". Senior: knows when it is consulted, task root defines task affinity, reparenting, and its role in avoiding or causing duplicate Recents cards.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A share-receiver activity inherited the default affinity and replaced the user's open session when sharing into the app; a dedicated affinity isolated it.

questions.promptHtml: How do you make a notification tap open a deep screen with a sensible Back history? What does TaskStackBuilder do and what does it require?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests knowledge of "regular" vs "special" activity entries and the synthesized back stack.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For an activity that is part of the normal app flow I build a PendingIntent with TaskStackBuilder, using addNextIntentWithParentStack(intent). It reads each activity's android:parentActivityName from the manifest, adds the whole parent chain, and starts it as a new task, so Back goes Detail → parent → … → Home rather than exiting the app. For a "special" activity that only exists via the notification, I use a plain PendingIntent with a separate task (NEW_TASK + CLEAR_TASK).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• TaskStackBuilder.create(context).addNextIntentWithParentStack(intent).getPendingIntent(requestCode, flags).
  • Parent chain comes from android:parentActivityName (API 16+) or, for AndroidX, getSupportParentActivityIntent() overrides. Missing metadata means only the target is pushed and Back exits.
  • The first intent of the synthesized stack is launched with NEW_TASK and CLEAR_TASK style flags (the builder sets them on the root), so tapping the notification replaces whatever task of this app was open, instead of adding on top. This is the standard behavior users see; make sure it is what you want.
  • Android 12+ (target 31+) restricts "notification trampolines": a notification tap cannot start a Service or BroadcastReceiver which then starts an activity. The PendingIntent must start the activity directly (PendingIntent.getActivity/the builder).
  • Android 12 (API 31) requires an explicit mutability flag on the PendingIntent: FLAG_IMMUTABLE (the usual choice); FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT if extras change. Request code identity is covered in the Intents chunk.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val detail = Intent(context, OrderDetailActivity::class.java).putExtra("id", orderId)
val pi = TaskStackBuilder.create(context)
    .addNextIntentWithParentStack(detail)
    .getPendingIntent(orderId.hashCode(), PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE)
val n = NotificationCompat.Builder(context, CHANNEL)
    .setContentIntent(pi).setAutoCancel(true).build()
<activity android:name=".OrderDetailActivity"
    android:parentActivityName=".OrdersActivity" />
<activity android:name=".OrdersActivity"
    android:parentActivityName=".MainActivity" />

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• No parentActivityName; Back leaves the app.
  • Same request code for different orders so the PendingIntent extras are overwritten.
  • Starting a trampoline Service/Receiver from the tap (blocked on Android 12+).
  • Forgetting that the root intent clears the existing task of this app.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Regular vs special activity? → Regular: part of the app flow, needs a synthetic stack. Special: only useful when reached from the notification; no parent stack.
  2. Why did Up differ from Back? → Up uses parentActivityName; Back uses the actual stack.
  3. What if the user is mid-checkout when the tap arrives? → Task is replaced; decide whether that is acceptable or use a non-clearing intent.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use TaskStackBuilder". Senior: manifest parent requirement, task-clearing side effect, trampoline ban, mutability flags, request codes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After moving the notification tap through a broadcast receiver for analytics, an Android 12 target bump silently stopped opening any screen; moving analytics into the activity fixed it.

questions.contextHtml: A messaging app (800K DAU, targetSdk 34) receives reports that tapping a chat notification opens the conversation, but pressing Back closes the app instead of showing the chat list (about 12% of notification taps, 3.1 stars in the last release notes). Crashlytics is clean. In the latest release the team replaced TaskStackBuilder with a simple PendingIntent.getActivity(..., ChatActivity) to "reduce complexity". Another change in the same release: ChatListActivity now declares taskAffinity="" to avoid a duplicate Recents card. Some users also say that when they were typing a message in the app and tapped a notification for another chat, the draft vanished.
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through diagnosis and the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Override onBackPressed in ChatActivity and launch the list." That hacks around symptoms, breaks Up navigation and predictive back, and ignores the second symptom (lost draft).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does Back misbehave only from notification taps, not from in-app navigation? Which release introduced it, and which flags does the PendingIntent use? Is parentActivityName still set for ChatActivity? Does it happen on cold app state and on warm?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix by restoring the TaskStackBuilder PendingIntent (staged rollout); this is a client-only change, no server involvement.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) a plain getActivity PendingIntent starts ChatActivity as the only activity in a new task, so Back exits; (b) parentActivityName is missing or points to an activity with a different affinity; (c) the task-clearing behavior on the builder replaces the open task, losing the draft; (d) red herring: notification channel or setAutoCancel.
  4. How I'd verify each: adb shell am start with the same intent and adb shell dumpsys activity activities to see the task contents; compare stacks from notification tap vs in-app. Review the notification code for flags. Check merged manifest for parentActivityName.
  5. Root cause: The simplification dropped the synthesized parent stack. Combined with an empty affinity on the list screen, the parent can't be joined anyway. And the draft loss comes from the builder's NEW_TASK|CLEAR_TASK on the root, which discards the existing task in the same app.
  6. Fix: short-term: restore TaskStackBuilder.addNextIntentWithParentStack with parentActivityName=.ChatListActivity, remove the empty affinity. Long-term: if the app is already in the foreground, avoid clearing: handle the tap with a single "NotificationRouterActivity" that checks whether the app task exists and uses CLEAR_TOP|SINGLE_TOP on the existing chat screen, or push the chat on top of the existing stack. Persist drafts to disk (draft table) so no flow depends on task survival.
  7. Prevention: an instrumentation test that taps a notification (UiAutomator) and asserts Back lands on the list; a manifest check for parentActivityName on notification target activities; add the stack dump to the notification QA checklist.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add a BroadcastReceiver trampoline to pick the behavior (blocked on Android 12+ targets and slower); I would not override Back to fake navigation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two chats notifications grouped; what does each PendingIntent need? → Distinct request codes (or distinct data URIs) and FLAG_IMMUTABLE.
  • App is currently on the same chat; tap its notification? → Prefer reusing with SINGLE_TOP so the user is not moved.
  • Cold process? → Stack still synthesizes; both entries are created lazily.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "cleanup" PR removed a TaskStackBuilder from an alerts feature because "it was just boilerplate". It passed all tests, since none tapped a notification. Support tickets about Back exiting the app were the first signal.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: overrides Back to patch.
  • Hire: diagnoses missing parent stack, restores TaskStackBuilder, uses dumpsys.
  • Strong hire: also identifies the task-clearing side effect, draft persistence, trampoline restrictions, and adds UI test coverage.

questions.contextHtml:
A single-activity app (2.2M DAU) uses show/hide fragment transactions for its 4 bottom tabs to keep scroll position. CartFragment handles Back to close an expanded bottom sheet. After a refactor, users on the Home tab report that Back does nothing for several taps until it finally exits (about 1 in 20 sessions, mostly users who visited Cart earlier). No crash, no ANR. Code:

class CartFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_cart) {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        requireActivity().onBackPressedDispatcher.addCallback(this) {
            sheet.collapse()   // runs even when sheet is already collapsed
        }
    }
}

Navigation to tabs is done with supportFragmentManager.beginTransaction().hide(current).show(next).commit().
questions.promptHtml: Why does Back do nothing on the Home tab, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Callback is leaking, remove it in onDestroy." Fragments with this as owner are already lifecycle-aware; the real issue is that a hidden fragment is still STARTED, so its callback is still active and LIFO ordering lets it win.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the callback unconditional (enabled all the time)? How are tabs switched (replace vs show/hide)? Does it repro only after visiting Cart? Does the fragment manager back stack get involved?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a one-line guard: callback isEnabled only when the sheet is expanded and the fragment is visible.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) show/hide leaves the hidden CartFragment STARTED/RESUMED, so its callback is registered and enabled; (b) callback logic swallows Back unconditionally; (c) FragmentManager's own back-stack callback is shadowed; (d) red herring: bottom-sheet state saved wrongly.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log the lifecycle of CartFragment on hide/show (no lifecycle callback changes on hide; only onHiddenChanged); add a log in handleOnBackPressed; adb shell dumpsys activity top shows fragment states; confirm that the callback fires on Home.
  5. Root cause: hide() does not move the fragment down the lifecycle (only the view visibility changes), so the callback registered with the fragment as lifecycle owner stays active. The dispatcher runs the most recent enabled callback first; Cart's callback consumes Back and does nothing useful.
  6. Fix:
private val callback = object : OnBackPressedCallback(false) {
    override fun handleOnBackPressed() { sheet.collapse() }
}
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    requireActivity().onBackPressedDispatcher.addCallback(this, callback)
}
private fun update() { callback.isEnabled = !isHidden && sheet.isExpanded }
override fun onHiddenChanged(hidden: Boolean) { update() }
// call update() from the sheet's state callback too

Long-term: replace show/hide with Navigation multiple back stacks or ViewPager2, which move fragments through lifecycle states properly. 7. Prevention: rule "a callback is enabled only when it can consume the event"; a test per tab that presses Back with no sheet open and asserts exit/previous tab. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use viewLifecycleOwner as the fix (a hidden view is still STARTED too); I would not remove callbacks manually in onStop.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Which callback wins if both Activity and Fragment register? → The most recently added enabled one.
  • Why not requireActivity().onBackPressed() inside? → Deprecated; with a still-enabled callback it re-enters the dispatcher.
  • What if the callback must run with predictive back animation? → Implement OnBackAnimationCallback-style progress via handleOnBackProgressed (Q224).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "dead Back" bug survived two releases because every QA repro started from a fresh install; the enabling condition required visiting a specific tab first. We found it by printing the dispatcher's enabled callbacks in a debug overlay.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: says leak and adds try/catch or manual remove.
  • Hire: explains that hidden fragments stay STARTED and fixes with isEnabled.
  • Strong hire: also gives LIFO order reasoning, the onHiddenChanged hook, and a proper architectural fix with tests.

questions.promptHtml: On Android 12 and above, pressing Back on the last launcher activity no longer destroys it. What exactly changed, and what code does it break?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is a silent platform behavior change that breaks session-end and cleanup logic placed in onDestroy.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Since Android 12 (API 31), when the user presses Back on a root launcher activity (the only activity in its task, with a MAIN/LAUNCHER intent filter), the system moves the task to the background instead of finishing the activity, so the activity goes to onStop and stays alive in memory like a Home press. This applies to all apps on Android 12+, regardless of targetSdk, unless the app overrides back handling. Code that assumed Back = onDestroy (ending sessions, stopping players, clearing state) stops running.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Rationale: users expect "Back = leave app" but the cold-start cost is high; keeping the process and activity gives faster relaunch (warm start).
  • Condition: the activity is the task root, is a launcher activity, and nothing else is above it. A root activity that is not a launcher, or any non-root, finishes as before.
  • Opt-out is by overriding: an app that handles back itself (overriding onBackPressed in Android 12 or registering an enabled OnBackPressedCallback) keeps its own behavior, and calling finish() yourself still finishes. Verify exact exclusion rules for the release you target on developer.android.com.
  • Effect on lifecycle: Back at root becomes onPause → onStop (no onDestroy). Returning is a hot start via onRestart → onStart → onResume.
  • Combined with predictive back's back-to-home animation, this is consistent: the user sees the app shrink to the launcher.
  • Fixes: move durable cleanup to onStop (and persist), observe ProcessLifecycleOwner, or end the session on a timeout; do not depend on onDestroy for correctness (not guaranteed anyway).
Android 11:  Back at root  -> onPause, onStop, onDestroy (activity gone)
Android 12+: Back at root  -> onPause, onStop            (task moved to back, activity alive)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Wrong: session ends only when the activity dies
override fun onDestroy() { super.onDestroy(); analytics.endSession() }

// Better: end the session when the app has been backgrounded for a grace period
ProcessLifecycleOwner.get().lifecycle.addObserver(LifecycleEventObserver { _, e ->
    if (e == Lifecycle.Event.ON_STOP) sessionTimer.start(30_000)
    if (e == Lifecycle.Event.ON_START) sessionTimer.cancel()
})

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Testing only on emulators of API 30 or below and missing it.
  • Assuming onDestroy runs when the user "leaves" the app.
  • Forgetting that stale UI state is shown on return; refresh data in onStart.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is this per targetSdk? → No; it is a platform behavior for apps running on Android 12+. The all-app/targetSdk distinction is covered in the behavior-changes chunk.
  2. How can I still exit? → Call finish()/finishAndRemoveTask() explicitly, but prefer not to; users expect the new behavior.
  3. Does it hold for non-launcher roots? → No; they finish normally.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it just minimises". Senior: names the exact condition, the lifecycle consequence (no onDestroy), the interaction with predictive back, and moves invariants off onDestroy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An analytics "session_end" event rate dropped 40% after Android 12 adoption because it fired in onDestroy.

questions.promptHtml: How do you control what appears in Recents? When would you use excludeFromRecents, autoRemoveFromRecents, finishAndRemoveTask, or documentLaunchMode?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Recents behaviors matter for privacy (sensitive screens), clean UX (transient tasks) and multi-document apps.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Recents shows tasks, so these controls apply per task via its root activity. android:excludeFromRecents="true" keeps the task out of Recents (useful for short-lived pickers, share receivers, or overlays). autoRemoveFromRecents removes the entry when its last activity finishes. finishAndRemoveTask() finishes the task and removes its card. documentLaunchMode lets one activity produce multiple Recents entries (one per document), implemented with NEW_DOCUMENT and MULTIPLE_TASK.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The attribute is read from the task's root activity. Putting excludeFromRecents on a non-root activity does nothing for the task card.
  • Runtime equivalents: FLAG_ACTIVITY_EXCLUDE_FROM_RECENTS on the launching intent, and ActivityManager.AppTask.setExcludeFromRecents() for the current task.
  • Privacy: Recents shows a thumbnail snapshot. FLAG_SECURE blanks it (and blocks screenshots). Since API 33 you can use Activity.setRecentsScreenshotEnabled(false) to hide only the Recents thumbnail without blocking screenshots.
  • Documents: android:documentLaunchMode="intoExisting" reuses the document task if the same document data is opened, "always" always creates a new task. The target should be reachable with data Uris distinguishing documents.
  • Related task attributes: clearTaskOnLaunch, finishOnTaskLaunch, alwaysRetainTaskState (these affect what the system discards when the user returns after a long idle; use sparingly).
  • Android 12 and up maxRecents (document tasks limit) exists, but I would verify values before relying on them.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<activity android:name=".PickerActivity"
    android:excludeFromRecents="true"
    android:autoRemoveFromRecents="true"
    android:taskAffinity="" />
class PaymentActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 33) setRecentsScreenshotEnabled(false)
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• excludeFromRecents on a screen deep inside the main flow: hides the whole task from users.
  • Using FLAG_SECURE just to hide a thumbnail, which also breaks screen sharing and accessibility tools.
  • Assuming the Recents card disappears when the user swipes it: swiping kills the task and often the process; do not rely on lifecycle callbacks there.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens to the process when swiped? → The task is removed and the process is typically killed (no lifecycle guarantee); OEMs differ.
  2. How do you hide a thumbnail only? → setRecentsScreenshotEnabled(false) API 33+, or FLAG_SECURE older/everywhere with side effects.
  3. Where is the root-only rule seen? → Attribute on non-root activity is ignored for card visibility.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "excludeFromRecents hides it". Senior: root-activity rule, privacy thumbnails, process kill on swipe, document mode.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A banking app's balance screen appeared in Recents thumbnails; setRecentsScreenshotEnabled replaced a FLAG_SECURE hack that had broken screen readers.

questions.contextHtml:
A fintech app (1.1M DAU) had a privacy incident: after Logout, pressing Back showed the previous user's account screen for about 0.3% of logouts (roughly 3,000 per day). Another group reported that after logging out and signing in as a different user, a stale "Statements" screen from the first user was visible in Recents. The logout code:

fun logout() {
    session.clear()
    startActivity(Intent(this, LoginActivity::class.java)
        .addFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK))
    finish()
}

StatementsActivity is opened from push notifications and from the share sheet via TaskStackBuilder, and has taskAffinity=".statements" so it appears as its own card. A security review is asking for a post-incident report.
questions.promptHtml: What were the causes, what did we ship, and how do we prevent recurrence?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add NEW_TASK." That is one cause out of three; it ignores the second task and the fact that screens must not rely on stack clearing for security.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the leak occur with logout from every screen or only some? Are there multiple tasks of the app in Recents (dumpsys)? Is the cached data in memory, ViewModel, or disk? Is the session clear observed by screens, or only checked at launch?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: on every Activity onStart, check session validity and redirect to Login if invalid; clear caches (in-memory repositories) at logout. Roll out as a priority release, with a server-side flag if possible.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) CLEAR_TASK without NEW_TASK is documented as invalid together; the task isn't reliably cleared; (b) StatementsActivity lives in a separate task via affinity, so clearing the main task never touches it; (c) data screens read cached state and don't re-check the session; (d) red herring: Recents thumbnail cache (cosmetic, but must be hidden for sensitive screens).
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce: open Statements via notification, logout from Main, Back. adb shell dumpsys activity activities | grep -E "Task|Activity" shows 2 tasks; inspect Recents. Unit/instrumentation test for logout across tasks.
  5. Root cause: Navigation-by-stack-clearing was the only protection. Wrong flags on one task and a second task that no flag ever reached left live authenticated screens.
  6. Fix: short-term:
fun Context.logout() {
    session.clear()
    startActivity(Intent(this, LoginActivity::class.java)
        .addFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK or Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK))
}
// BaseActivity
override fun onStart() { super.onStart(); if (!session.isActive) finishAndRemoveTask() }

Long-term: model the session as state (StateFlow) that all authenticated activities observe and finish themselves on sign-out; clear in-memory caches; setRecentsScreenshotEnabled(false) or FLAG_SECURE on sensitive screens; remove the custom affinity (or give it only for non-authenticated pickers). 7. Prevention: instrumentation test "logout from each entry point (launcher, notification, share) and press Back"; threat model item "session end ≠ UI navigation"; code review checklist for flags. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not rely on finishAffinity() alone (it only finishes activities in the same task affinity chain); I would not delay the fix to redesign navigation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not finishAffinity()? → It finishes activities in the current task with the same affinity; not other tasks.
  • Session token expired in the background? → The onStart guard handles it without a logout action.
  • Multi-window with two app windows? → Each task observes the session flow; both finish.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A healthcare-adjacent app discovered through a support ticket that a share target kept patient data visible in Recents after sign-out; the fix was a session observer and a unit test per entry point, not another flag.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds NEW_TASK and stops.
  • Hire: finds the second task via affinity, adds a session guard.
  • Strong hire: separates security from navigation, handles Recents thumbnails and caches, adds multi-entry tests and a postmortem action list.

questions.promptHtml: Explain predictive back: how do you opt in, what changes for your code, and how has enforcement changed from Android 13 to 16?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the biggest back-navigation change in a decade and breaks apps that rely on onBackPressed, onKeyDown, or custom navigation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Predictive back lets the user peek at the destination during the back gesture and cancel it. It requires callbacks registered ahead of time rather than an after-the-fact onBackPressed. I opt in with android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback="true" (application or per activity), register OnBackPressedCallbacks, and for custom animations implement progress callbacks (handleOnBackStarted/Progressed/Cancelled, AndroidX Activity 1.6+). It began as a developer-option preview on Android 13 (API 33), got in-app and cross-activity/task animations on 14, and the system animations moved out of developer options on 15. For apps targeting Android 16 (API 36) the behavior is on by default and legacy onBackPressed/KEYCODE_BACK callbacks are no longer invoked; verify details and opt-out status on developer.android.com.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Platform API: OnBackInvokedDispatcher.registerOnBackInvokedCallback(priority, callback) (API 33); OnBackAnimationCallback (API 34) with onBackStarted/Progressed/Cancelled/Invoked.
  • AndroidX bridges: OnBackPressedCallback has handleOnBackStarted(BackEventCompat), handleOnBackProgressed, handleOnBackCancelled (activity 1.6+). Fragment/AndroidX Navigation 2.7+ and Compose (PredictiveBackHandler, material components) build on it.
  • System animations: back-to-home (always possible when no callback intercepts), cross-activity, cross-task. The system uses whether any enabled callback exists to decide: if yes, your code handles it; if no, the system animation plays and then the activity finishes.
  • Consequences: do not use onKeyDown(KEYCODE_BACK) or onBackPressed(); callbacks must be enabled only when they truly intercept; state-driven isEnabled. Custom Dialog/PopupWindow/DialogFragment have their own dispatchers.
  • Migration pitfalls: third-party libraries that override dispatchKeyEvent for Back, custom frameworks that intercept Back centrally, and unconditional callbacks that block system animation.
Gesture starts -> system asks: any enabled callback?
   yes -> callback.onBackStarted / Progressed(progress 0..1) / Invoked or Cancelled
   no  -> system animation (home / cross-activity / cross-task), then finish

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<application android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback="true" />
<!-- or per <activity>, to migrate one screen at a time -->
val cb = object : OnBackPressedCallback(true) {
    override fun handleOnBackStarted(e: BackEventCompat) { panel.beginPeek() }
    override fun handleOnBackProgressed(e: BackEventCompat) { panel.peek(e.progress) }
    override fun handleOnBackPressed() { panel.close() }
    override fun handleOnBackCancelled() { panel.cancelPeek() }
}
onBackPressedDispatcher.addCallback(this, cb)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Opting in while still overriding onBackPressed; the override is never called.
  • Callback always enabled (blocks system animation, defeats the feature).
  • Testing only with gesture navigation off; three-button navigation also dispatches via callbacks but has no peek.
  • Assuming version numbers: enforcement is "opt-in by manifest" for older targets, default for target 36 (verify).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do I test it? → Developer options "Predictive back animations" on 13/14, Android 15+ on by default for opted-in apps; Espresso pressBack/pressBackUnconditionally; Compose OnBackPressedDispatcher tests.
  2. What about dialogs? → Dialogs and sheets register their own callback with PRIORITY_OVERLAY; use library components that support it.
  3. What breaks with KeyEvent handlers? → They are not dispatched for Back when opted in/targeting 36.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "new back animation". Senior: explains why callbacks must be registered ahead, state-driven enable, per-version rollout, and plans a staged migration.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After opting in, a payment confirmation screen lost its "are you sure?" dialog because the logic lived in onBackPressed; a code audit before the switch would have caught it.

questions.promptHtml: What are the options for animating between activities, and what changed with overridePendingTransition in recent releases? Name the common pitfalls with shared element transitions.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests practical UI-plumbing knowledge and awareness of API deprecations.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: There are three layers: simple enter/exit animations (overridePendingTransition, deprecated in API 34 in favor of overrideActivityTransition(OVERRIDE_TRANSITION_OPEN/CLOSE, enter, exit)), window content transitions (Material container transform / fade), and shared element transitions using ActivityOptions.makeSceneTransitionAnimation. Predictive back's cross-activity animation uses the system's own transition and can conflict with custom ones, so on newer releases I'd prefer theme-defined or Material transitions.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• overridePendingTransition(enter, exit) must be called right after startActivity/finish. In API 34 it is deprecated; overrideActivityTransition (API 34) separates open and close animations and works for back gestures too.
  • Window animations can also be set in the theme (windowAnimationStyle), applying to all activities uniformly.
  • Content transitions: window.requestFeature(FEATURE_ACTIVITY_TRANSITIONS) (default with Material themes), Window.enterTransition, exitTransition; start with ActivityOptions.makeSceneTransitionAnimation(activity, view, "shared_name").toBundle().
  • Shared elements: unique transitionName per view. In a list the names must be per item ("image_$id"). The destination should call postponeEnterTransition() until the shared view is laid out and the image loaded, then startPostponedEnterTransition(); otherwise the animation jumps or flickers.
  • Material Components: MaterialContainerTransform and MaterialSharedAxis give consistent motion.
  • Compose / Navigation 3 has its own transition APIs (covered under the Compose chunk); across activity boundaries you still need the framework APIs above.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// API 34+
overrideActivityTransition(Activity.OVERRIDE_TRANSITION_OPEN, R.anim.slide_in, R.anim.fade_out)
overrideActivityTransition(Activity.OVERRIDE_TRANSITION_CLOSE, R.anim.fade_in, R.anim.slide_out)

// Shared element
val opts = ActivityOptions.makeSceneTransitionAnimation(this, thumb, "image_$id")
startActivity(Intent(this, DetailActivity::class.java).putExtra("id", id), opts.toBundle())

// DetailActivity
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    postponeEnterTransition()
    heroImage.load(url) { listener(onSuccess = { _, _ -> startPostponedEnterTransition() }) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling overridePendingTransition before startActivity (no effect).
  • Duplicate transitionNames across list items.
  • Forgetting startPostponedEnterTransition(): screen appears frozen for ~ the transition timeout.
  • Heavy work in onCreate delaying the first frame and making the animation stutter.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you animate back? → overrideActivityTransition(CLOSE...), theme, or finishAfterTransition().
  2. Why does the shared element sometimes not animate on back? → Return transition needs the same name and the list view recycled to the same position; use setEnterSharedElementCallback to remap.
  3. How does predictive back interact? → The system cross-activity animation takes precedence in gesture navigation unless you opt out; test both.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "overridePendingTransition". Senior: knows the API 34 replacement, postpone/start for shared elements, uniqueness of names, and the predictive back interplay.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A gallery app's shared-element animation janked on mid-range devices because the full-resolution image decoded on the main thread before startPostponedEnterTransition; moving to a pre-decoded thumbnail fixed it.

questions.contextHtml: A marketplace app (3M DAU) sends product links in emails and WhatsApp shares. ProductActivity is standard. Analytics shows 4.5% of deep-link sessions end up with the same product screen stacked 2-3 times; Back from the last one shows the same product again, and users abandon (bounce up 6 points on those sessions). Memory warnings also rise on low-end 2 GB devices because each product screen holds a gallery. Intent filter has autoVerify app links. Android Studio's Navigation graph is used inside the Product flow. Red herrings reported: "only on Android 13", "only when the app was already open", "happens more after the new image carousel".
questions.promptHtml: How do you diagnose and fix this?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make ProductActivity singleTask." That kills the stack above Main on every link (loses the browsing history), breaks multi-product comparison, and does not explain why it only happens sometimes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which sources open the link (browser, email app, WhatsApp, in-app web view)? Is the app foregrounded or in the background, and what is on top of the stack when the link arrives? Do the duplicates have the same product id? Is the intent started with NEW_TASK by the source app (I cannot control that)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add singleTop to ProductActivity plus handling in onNewIntent for the "same product on top" case; ship fast, it's safe and small.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) standard launch creates a new instance every time a link arrives while a product screen is already on top, or deeper; (b) the source launches with NEW_TASK, which re-enters the app's existing task and adds another copy on top; (c) in-app navigation pushes the same product repeatedly (similar-products carousel), indistinguishable in the stack; (d) red herring: Android 13 or carousel (memory only amplifies the effect).
  4. How I'd verify each: Send links with adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "https://shop.example/p/42" repeatedly, with the app in each state, and dump stacks with dumpsys activity activities; add a debug log of intent.flags and isTaskRoot in onCreate; check whether the duplicates have equal ids.
  5. Root cause: standard means no deduplication; singleTop only dedupes when the instance is on top. External apps decide the launch flags, so the manifest is the only guard I control. The stack [Main, Product(42), Product(42)] appears when a link for 42 arrives while 42 is on top without singleTop; [Main, Product(42), Product(7), Product(42)] is allowed and legitimate.
  6. Fix: short-term: singleTop and in onNewIntent call setIntent and apply the id (reload if different). Long-term: a deep link router activity or a single host activity:
// Router: one place that owns the policy
class DeepLinkRouterActivity : Activity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        val product = Intent(this, ProductActivity::class.java)
            .setData(intent.data)
        TaskStackBuilder.create(this)
            .addNextIntentWithParentStack(product)
            .startActivities()
        finish()
    }
}

Use CLEAR_TOP | SINGLE_TOP for "same destination" semantics inside the app, and cap the stack depth (e.g. replace the top when navigating product to product from the carousel). 7. Prevention: instrumentation tests per source state (cold, warm same product, warm different product); a launch-mode review in the manifest checklist; a dashboard metric "activities per task" in debug builds via ActivityLifecycleCallbacks. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use singleTask (destroys browsing context); I would not use singleInstance; I would not drop NEW_TASK handling since I do not control the sender.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the link is for a different product while 42 is on top? → With singleTop it reuses and swaps the content; decide whether that is the desired UX (replace vs push).
  • Chrome custom tab hands off? → Behavior depends on how the browser launches the intent; verify on the target browsers.
  • Process killed in the background? → New process; one instance only, restored from the system stack.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A promo campaign multiplied deep-link traffic 5x and doubled the duplicate rate; a router activity that owned launch policy removed the class of bug rather than patching individual screens.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests singleTask blindly.
  • Hire: singleTop plus onNewIntent, reproduces via adb.
  • Strong hire: understands who controls flags, uses a router/stack builder, discusses UX of product-to-product navigation and tests across states.

questions.subtopic: How the system picks a task
questions.promptHtml: Describe how the system decides which task and which instance to use when I call startActivity. Walk through the decision for launchMode, flags and affinity.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who can narrate the algorithm can predict behavior rather than memorize tables.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The ActivityTaskManager (ActivityStarter) merges the target's launchMode and the intent flags into one effective set of launch flags, then decides: does this launch need a new task (NEW_TASK, singleTask, singleInstance, or a non-activity caller)? If so, it looks for an existing task with a matching affinity or root intent; if none, it creates one. Within the chosen task it applies instance rules: singleTop (top only), singleTask / CLEAR_TOP (find existing, clear above, deliver onNewIntent), CLEAR_TASK (empty first), else create a new instance on top.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
1. Compute effective flags: manifest mode is translated (singleTask → implies NEW_TASK semantics; singleInstance → exclusive task). Caller-supplied flags are merged, with the caller usually unable to weaken what the manifest requires.
  2. Caller type: if the caller is not an Activity (no task), NEW_TASK is required (else exception).
  3. Find a target task: for new-task launches, search recent tasks for one whose affinity matches the target's taskAffinity, or whose root/base intent matches the component. Found → bring to front. Not found → create a task with the target as root.
  4. Within the task, look for an existing instance (for singleTask, CLEAR_TOP, singleTop checks): the top (singleTop), or any (singleTask / CLEAR_TOP). If found, optionally clear above, then deliver the intent (onNewIntent) or recreate it (standard + CLEAR_TOP without SINGLE_TOP).
  5. Else create the instance, push it on top.
  6. Lifecycle: the previous top pauses before the new one resumes; stop happens after the new activity is visible.
  • Edge cases: MULTIPLE_TASK forces a new task even with matching affinity; RESET_TASK_IF_NEEDED, clearTaskOnLaunch and finishOnTaskLaunch change what is dropped when returning to an old task; documents have per-document tasks.
  • I would treat this as the model, not as exact AOSP code; to be exact, read ActivityStarter and ActivityTaskSupervisor in AOSP for the release you target.
startActivity
  -> merge manifest mode + flags
  -> need new task? --no--> use caller's task
       | yes: find task by affinity/root --found--> bring to front
       |                                  --none--> create task
  -> inside task: reuse instance? (top / any / clear above)
        yes -> onNewIntent (or recreate)     no -> new instance on top

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Exploration harness for interviews and debugging: dump the result of each combination
// adb shell am start -n pkg/.Product --activity-clear-top --activity-single-top
// adb shell dumpsys activity activities | grep -E "Task|ActivityRecord"

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking singleTask only checks the caller's task.
  • Thinking flags always override launchMode.
  • Forgetting that the previous activity's onStop can be delayed until the new one draws.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if two tasks match? → The system picks the most recent matching task.
  2. Why does NEW_TASK sometimes not create a new task? → Because a matching task exists.
  3. What about multi-window? → Each window has its own task; MULTIPLE_TASK and singleInstancePerTask let you open another window with a new instance.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: a table. Senior: a pipeline: flags merged, new-task decision, lookup by affinity/root, instance reuse, lifecycle; and the ability to verify with dumpsys.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An email app launching our deep links with NEW_TASK looked random to the team until the pipeline made it obvious.

questions.subtopic: Choosing launch modes for multi-entry apps
questions.contextHtml: You are the tech lead for a social app (6M DAU) moving from 14 activities to one MainActivity hosting Compose Navigation. Entry points: launcher, push notifications (5 types), deep links from web, a share target (images and text), app shortcuts, and a home-screen widget. Requirements from product: (1) tapping a notification never throws away the user's in-progress compose screen without warning; (2) Back from a share target returns to the app that shared; (3) deep links always land on the right screen with a sensible Back path; (4) no duplicate Main in Recents. Today, Main is standard. Some teammates want singleTask, others singleTop.
questions.promptHtml: Pick a design and defend the trade-offs.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "singleTask because it prevents duplicates." Ignores requirement (2) and (1): singleTask with a matching task brings the whole app task to the front and clears everything above Main, and Back won't return to the sharing app.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What state must survive a notification (draft persisted or only in memory)? Is the share target a separate screen or into Main? Do we support multi-window or large screens (multiple instances)? What is the minSdk (singleInstancePerTask needs 31)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; a decision with a staged rollout and a flag to roll back launch behavior.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (options): (a) Main singleTop with a fixed CLEAR_TOP|SINGLE_TOP start from our own PendingIntents; (b) Main singleTask; (c) Main standard plus a trampoline Router; (d) separate ShareReceiverActivity with its own affinity and singleInstancePerTask.
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype each and run a matrix of entry points × states (cold, warm in Home, warm mid-compose, warm in another app) with UiAutomator and dumpsys activity activities; count Recents cards and check Back targets.
  5. Root cause: n/a; the trade is between deduplication and preserving user context and caller return.
  6. Fix (decision): Main singleTop. Own PendingIntents use FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK|CLEAR_TOP|SINGLE_TOP only when the app is not in compose mode; a navigation layer in onNewIntent handles deep links by pushing destinations with a synthesized parent chain (Navigation's handleDeepLink/NavDeepLinkBuilder) and asks for confirmation when the destination would discard drafts (drafts are also persisted to disk). The share target is a dedicated lightweight activity (taskAffinity="", excludeFromRecents, autoRemoveFromRecents) that stores the payload and offers "Open in app"; Back returns to the sharing app naturally because it launches in the caller's task or its own.
  7. Prevention: automated entry-point matrix tests; Recents card count asserted; a doc of launch policy next to the manifest; telemetry for "activities per task".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: singleTask gives dedupe but destroys context and Back-to-caller; singleInstance is wrong for the host; a router adds a hop (a few ms, an extra activity), and cannot be used as a notification trampoline (Android 12+), so the router must be the direct target of the PendingIntent.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Large screens with two windows of the app? → Allow it with singleInstancePerTask on API 31+ for the host, or keep it singleTop and do not support multi-instance (state a product decision).
  • Widget taps while process is dead? → New process; handle in onCreate; both paths use the same router function.
  • Google Play policy or OEM launch weirdness? → Use adb matrix on key OEMs; avoid depending on caller flags.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team picked singleTask for its host activity and later discovered that share-to-app flows no longer returned to the source app; the "fix" required a separate receiver activity, which should have been the first design.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks a mode by slogan.
  • Hire: weighs singleTop vs singleTask against stated requirements.
